title: ProCARE: Real-World Study Automation via Profile-Grounded Evidence Contracts
authors: Zhaoyu Fan, Bowen Han, Jincheng Ou, Yanwei Ren, Zehua He, Kaiyu Huang
abstract: Real-world studies (RWS) analyze routinely collected healthcare data, such as electronic health records and insurance claims, to estimate treatment effects, monitor safety, and identify risk factors outside randomized trials. Automating RWS with large language model agents is appealing but brittle: valid analyses depend on dataset-specific clinical semantics, including index dates, follow-up windows, patient/event-level units, and outcome boundaries that are often implicit in observational data. This leads to schema mismatches, temporal errors, inconsistent analytical granularity, and unsupported clinical claims. We present ProCARE, a profile-grounded framework that reformulates RWS automation as constrained compilation. ProCARE converts heterogeneous data profiles into Evidence Contracts specifying available variables, temporal attributes, distributions, and evidentiary limits, and compiles study objectives into RWS-IR, a strongly typed intermediate representation for variables, time relations, analysis units, and statistical tasks. Deterministic validation and localized repair then check and revise generated workflows across schema mapping, cohort construction, variable derivation, analysis, and interpretation. On 36 EHR-based benchmark tasks, ProCARE outperforms strong LLM-agent baselines in code executability, semantic consistency, and conclusion traceability, with automated violation diagnoses showing moderate-to-substantial agreement with blinded expert review.

infographic.key_insight: ProCARE turns real-world study automation into a constrained compilation problem by grounding LLM agents in dataset-specific evidence contracts and a typed intermediate representation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could make AI-generated observational research workflows more reliable for treatment effects, safety monitoring, and risk-factor studies using EHR or claims data.
method: Converts heterogeneous data profiles into Evidence Contracts with variables, temporal attributes, distributions, and evidentiary limits.
Compiles study goals into RWS-IR, a strongly typed format for variables, time relations, analysis units, and statistical tasks.
Uses deterministic validation and localized repair to catch and fix schema, cohort, analysis, and interpretation errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 36 EHR-based benchmark tasks, ProCARE improved code executability, semantic consistency, and conclusion traceability versus strong LLM-agent baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and completeness of dataset profiling, and the approach still needs careful human oversight for unsupported clinical claims.
infographic.paper_title: ProCARE: Real-World Study Automation via Profile-Grounded Evidence Contracts

title: The Federated Tumor Segmentation and Classification (FeTS++) Challenge
authors: Wenyi Tang, Carla Pitarch-Abaigar, Siddhesh Thakur, Verena Chung, Konstantinos Koukoutegos, Alexandros Karargyris
abstract: International challenges have become the standard for developing and benchmarking biomedical image analysis methods using centralized multi-institutional data. Federated learning (FL) describes a paradigm-shift on multi-institutional collaborations, where models are trained across institutions while their data are always retained locally. The Federated Tumor Segmentation (FeTS) challenge, first held in 2021, was the first challenge dedicated to FL in medical imaging and editions in 2022 and 2024 pushed the frontiers of real-world method validation. FeTS++ 2027 returns after a two-year gap with a substantially larger and more diverse cohort, and with the two "pluses" that name the challenge: an official classification task alongside segmentation, and a move of the infrastructure to NVIDIA FLARE (NVFlare). Built on the clinically acquired, multi-institutional multi-parametric MRI data of the BraTS 2025 Lighthouse challenge, FeTS++ spans gliomas and meningiomas across patient cohorts from institutions in North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, and focuses on ranking submitted methodological approaches according to their model utility and an efficiency-aware score. Task 1 asks participants to find the best strategy for aggregating knowledge from per-institution segmentation models, while Task 2 asks them to distinguish glioma from meningioma under the same federated protocol, in which the entity label is heavily confounded with the site of origin.

infographic.key_insight: FeTS++ 2027 expands federated medical imaging benchmarking by adding a federated classification task and moving the challenge infrastructure to NVFlare across a larger, more diverse multi-institutional cohort.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The challenge aims to improve how tumor segmentation and tumor-type classification models are developed across hospitals without centralizing patient data, supporting more realistic deployment of AI in neuro-oncology.
method: Federated learning across institutions with data kept locally
Task 1: aggregate per-institution segmentation models for tumor segmentation
Task 2: classify glioma vs meningioma under the same federated protocol
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a multi-institutional MRI dataset spanning North America, Europe, Asia, and Africa, with methods ranked by model utility and an efficiency-aware score.
infographic.watch_item: Classification is heavily confounded by site of origin, so site bias and cross-institution generalization are major concerns when interpreting results.
infographic.paper_title: The Federated Tumor Segmentation and Classification (FeTS++) Challenge

title: SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation
authors: Ziyang Song, Lia Shen, Yixuan Li, Qincheng Lu, Weihao Li, Haoran Xu
abstract: Biomedical language models (LMs) provide strong representations for clinical tasks, but they often fail to capture the hierarchical structure among medical concepts. This limitation is especially pronounced for rare and fine-grained clinical codes in long-tailed vocabularies, where hierarchy-agnostic LM representations become less informative as concept frequency decreases. We introduce Semantic Medical Identifier (SMI), a training-free framework for constructing ontology-grounded Semantic IDs and hierarchy-aware medical concept representations. For each diagnosis, procedure, or medication concept, SMI defines its Semantic ID as the coarse-to-fine path through an expert-defined medical ontology. SMI then aggregates frozen biomedical LM embeddings across the corresponding ontology levels to form hierarchy-aware medical concept representations that preserve coarse-to-fine clinical semantics. The base SMI uses uniform aggregation across ontology levels, while a level-weighted variant selects global level weights on validation data. Our theoretical analysis shows that SMI yields more informative medical concept representations than hierarchy-agnostic LM embeddings, particularly for rare and fine-grained clinical concepts. Experiments show that SMI captures meaningful hierarchical structure and improves clinical relation prediction. On MIMIC-IV, SMI improves mortality prediction, readmission prediction, drug recommendation, and rare drug prediction. On eICU, SMI yields more robust patient representations under cross-hospital distribution shift.

infographic.key_insight: SMI turns each medical concept into an ontology-based coarse-to-fine semantic path and uses it to build hierarchy-aware representations that are especially helpful for rare, fine-grained codes.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could improve downstream clinical prediction and recommendation by making biomedical models better reflect medical hierarchies instead of treating codes as unrelated labels.
method: Define each diagnosis, procedure, or medication as a Semantic ID from an expert ontology path
Aggregate frozen biomedical LM embeddings across ontology levels to create concept representations
Optionally learn level weights on validation data for a weighted variant
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on MIMIC-IV and eICU show improved mortality, readmission, drug recommendation, rare drug prediction, and better robustness under cross-hospital shift.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and coverage of the underlying medical ontology, and validation-tuned level weights may not transfer equally well across institutions or coding systems.
infographic.paper_title: SMI: Ontology-Grounded Semantic IDs for Hierarchy-Aware Medical Concept Representation

title: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining
authors: Joshua Placidi, Inigo Stibbe, Alfred J. Balston, Marek Rei, A. Aldo Faisal
abstract: Autoregressive electronic health record (EHR) foundation models predict the next event token in patient trajectories: sequences of structured medical events. A typical pretraining strategy is to concatenate all trajectories into a global stream and sample token windows from it. This gives patients with longer sequences more training exposure and allows tokens to attend across patient boundaries. We argue that these choices create a misalignment between pretraining and downstream clinical tasks. To explore this, we investigate how the composition of pretraining sequences affects clinical prediction performance. Using the global-stream approach as a baseline, we propose alternative sequence composition methods that control how patient trajectories contribute to pretraining sequences. Across four MIMIC-IV v2.2 tasks, our best method improves macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, with relative gains of 9.3% in F1 and 2.7% in AUPRC under a fixed training recipe. We find that these gains generalize across four additional evaluation settings, including the INSPIRE and eICU-CRD datasets, with improvements in macro AUROC, AUPRC, and F1 score. Our results show that simply changing how EHR data are presented to the model during pretraining can improve downstream performance, without changing the model or collecting additional data.

infographic.key_insight: How patient records are grouped during EHR model pretraining can materially improve downstream clinical prediction, even without changing the model architecture or adding data.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A better pretraining sequence format may help foundation models produce more accurate risk predictions across common hospital datasets and tasks.
method: Compared a global-stream pretraining baseline against alternative ways of composing patient sequences.
Controlled how much each patient trajectory contributes to training windows.
Evaluated effects on multiple clinical prediction benchmarks under the same training recipe.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four MIMIC-IV v2.2 tasks and four additional evaluation settings, the best method improved macro AUROC, AUPRC, F1, and balanced accuracy, including gains of 9.3% in F1 and 2.7% in AUPRC.
infographic.watch_item: Results are benchmark-specific, so real-world benefit may depend on the dataset, task mix, and how sequences are constructed in deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Sequence Composition in EHR Foundation Model Pretraining

title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts
authors: Boya Zhang, Yuanchao Ma, Jiageng Wu, Krittaphas Chaisutyakorn, Rodrigo Gameiro, Ahram Han
abstract: Pain is one of the most common and clinically important symptoms, reflecting disease onset, progression, and treatment response. However, pain is difficult to accurately capture and interpret from medical text, as its expression varies across languages, documentation types, and patient demographics, and is often embedded in terminology, negation, temporality, and contextual descriptions. Existing pain-related studies remain largely monolingual or limited to narrow clinical settings. In this study, we introduce PAINT, a multilingual framework for studying pain representation across medical exams and real-world clinical texts. PAINT includes nine pain-focused dataset partitions spanning English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, with clinician annotations in all four languages. We curated a structured schema covering pain relevance, pain presence, anatomical location, pain descriptors, and demographic information. To capture multilingual pain representations, we leverage large language models (LLMs) and adopt an ensemble strategy to improve performance. Ten clinicians across four languages validate the labels: the ensemble reaches macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 on pain relevance and pain presence and 92-100% accuracy on demographics, with inter-annotator $κ$ of 0.82-1.00. We release the WorldMedQA-Pain ensemble labels, the extraction pipeline, validation scripts, and clinician annotation sheets for publicly licensed corpora, providing a foundation for pain-centered clinical NLP and for studying pain documentation across languages and healthcare contexts.

infographic.key_insight: PAINT is a multilingual framework that standardizes how pain is identified and described across medical exam questions and real-world clinical text in English, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese.
infographic.clinical_relevance: By improving pain extraction across languages and documentation styles, PAINT can support more consistent symptom understanding for clinical NLP, research, and cross-language health data analysis.
method: Curated nine pain-focused dataset partitions across medical licensing exams and clinical texts.
Built a structured annotation schema for pain relevance, pain presence, location, descriptors, and demographics.
Used large language models with an ensemble strategy, then validated labels with clinicians across four languages.
infographic.evidence_signal: The ensemble achieved macro-F1 of 0.91-1.00 for pain relevance and pain presence, 92-100% accuracy for demographics, and inter-annotator κ of 0.82-1.00.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was validated on publicly licensed corpora and may not fully generalize to all specialties, languages, or local documentation practices.
infographic.paper_title: PAINT: A Framework for Multilingual Pain Representation from Medical Licensing Exams to Real-World Clinical Texts

title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning
authors: Li-Ching Chen, Andrés Franco Valiente, Yuta Ishiyama, Zachary R. Chalmers, William Chen, Kelsey Natsuhara
abstract: Clinical decision-making is a sequential process of information collection, clinical inference, and forecasting under partial observability, often without a uniquely correct treatment decision. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong medical question-answering capabilities but extending these advances to clinical reasoning remains challenging because many clinical tasks are only partially verifiable. Recent clinical reinforcement learning (RL) work has therefore largely focused on diagnostic endpoints, where correctness can be more directly verified. Oncology treatment decision making is a particularly challenging instance of this problem that extends beyond medical question-answering in which multiple decision trajectories can be clinically defensible for the same partially observed patient state. We formulate oncology treatment planning as an interactive RL problem under partial observability and construct patient-specific, process-aware rewards from decision processes observed in real world clinical records. The agent must learn to sequentially acquire information from a structured patient representation before committing to a first-line treatment recommendation, and is evaluated on information gathering, treatment selection, and reasoning alignment. Using GRPO and GDPO to optimize Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct within this environment, RL substantially improves the base policy beyond frontier model capabilities. The GDPO-trained policy increases Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by $79.60\%$ over base Llama and exceeds GPT-5.2 by $18.82\%$ under the same interactive environment, while reducing query count during training. Overall, our results show that patient-specific, partially verifiable rewards can provide an effective learning signal for interactive clinical RL when both the patient state and the underlying clinical decision process are only partially observed.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that reinforcement learning can improve an LLM’s oncology treatment planning by learning from partially verifiable, patient-specific rewards rather than relying only on fully correct answers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may better support real-world cancer decision support, where multiple treatment paths can be reasonable and clinicians must first gather information before choosing a therapy.
method: Formulated colon cancer treatment planning as an interactive RL task under partial observability.
Built process-aware rewards from real-world clinical records to score information gathering, reasoning, and treatment selection.
Optimized Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with GRPO and GDPO and compared performance against frontier models.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the abstract, the GDPO-trained policy improved Mean@3 scalar clinical reward by 79.60% over base Llama and outperformed GPT-5.2 by 18.82% in the same interactive environment.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from an interactive evaluation environment, so clinical deployment would still require careful validation for safety, generalizability, and real-world workflow fit.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning In Partially Verifiable Environments for Colon Cancer Treatment Planning

title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation
authors: Rui Tang, Hongqiu Wang
abstract: Healthcare agents must transform longitudinal clinical evidence into reliable actions through heterogeneous tools and stateful workflows, conditions under which model-centric systems may lose context, misuse tools, fail to verify consequential transitions, or cross authorization boundaries. Existing medical-agent benchmarks primarily emphasize terminal task outcomes, making it difficult to determine whether execution failures arise from the agent model, the runtime harness, or their interaction. We present the Medical Harness Protocol, an outcome-preserving framework that independently evaluates seven healthcare-specific process dimensions: Care Action Fulfillment, Clinical Resource Competence, Patient-Evidence Alignment, Clinical Workflow Continuity, Clinical Auditability, Closed-Loop Verification, and Clinical Conduct Boundaries. A normalized intervention trace further tracks whether runtime support is available, activated, delivered, adopted by the agent, and propagated into subsequent behavior. We instantiate the protocol as MedHarnessBench, comprising 342 executable tasks across FHIR/EHR operations, healthcare-administration interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools. Across more than 16,000 controlled task executions, MedHarness yields broad improvements in terminal task success, intermediate subtask completion, and healthcare-specific process quality. We further evaluate MedHarness against multiple general-purpose harnesses and use controlled single-fault perturbations to verify the sensitivity and discrimination of the seven-dimensional evaluation. These results demonstrate that healthcare-specific runtime support can substantially improve both task completion and execution quality, while revealing failures that terminal outcomes alone cannot capture. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/Tomry1114/Awesome-Agent-Harness-for-Healthcare.

infographic.key_insight: MedHarnessBench shows that healthcare-specific runtime support can improve agent task success and reveal process failures that terminal outcomes miss.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For healthcare AI systems, evaluating how agents use tools, follow workflows, and respect boundaries is crucial for safer, more reliable deployment.
method: Defined the Medical Harness Protocol to score seven healthcare process dimensions.
Built MedHarnessBench with 342 executable tasks spanning FHIR/EHR, admin interfaces, and multimodal clinical tools.
Ran more than 16,000 controlled executions and compared against general-purpose harnesses with single-fault perturbations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark reports broad gains in terminal success, subtask completion, and process quality across over 16,000 controlled task executions.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from benchmarked executions, so real-world performance may differ when tools, data quality, and clinical workflows are less controlled.
infographic.paper_title: MedHarnessBench: A Unified Benchmark for Healthcare Agent Evaluation

title: ClinEdge: An Expert-Graded Benchmark of Real Patient Edge Cases Where Frontier Multimodal Models Fail
authors: Anurag Sharma, Aditya Sharma, Sapna Baalwan
abstract: Most benchmarks for large language models in medicine are built from licensing examinations and theoretical questions. The few that draw on real clinical data do so only in part, and rarely require a model to read a patient's own imaging. ClinEdge addresses this gap with 32 real, de-identified patient cases from active clinical practice, each evaluated across seven frontier systems for a total of 224 expert-graded evaluations. Each case pairs primary imaging with a short vignette, contains a feature known to defeat pattern-matched reasoning, and is scored against the patient's documented clinical course. The suite is built for depth rather than volume. Grading followed a two-stage expert process. First, a senior orthopaedic surgeon graded all 224 responses on a weighted rubric and a pass-or-fail verdict. Second, a panel of nineteen physicians, largely senior specialists at teaching medical colleges, independently reviewed every case and every one of the 224 grades. All seven production systems were evaluated through their public interfaces, and all 224 conversations are preserved as replayable links. Performance was poor across all systems, and the failures were shared: different vendors missed the same findings and converged on the same wrong plans. From the experts' notes we catalogue 18 recurring failure modes in five families. The models stop reading an image at the first finding. They give generic plans and lean toward over-treatment. They trust a misleading history over correct imaging. Their answers vary across systems and runs, and change with question format. Failing answers were delivered fluently and without any expressed uncertainty. Four cases are released in full; the remaining 28 are held out, and we invite frontier AI labs and healthcare AI companies to evaluate their models against them (research@futrbridge.com)

infographic.key_insight: ClinEdge shows that frontier multimodal models can fail on real patient imaging cases in consistent, clinically meaningful ways, especially when cases include misleading or edge-case findings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark highlights that model outputs may look fluent but still miss key imaging findings, overstate certainty, and suggest inappropriate plans, underscoring the need for careful expert oversight in medical imaging use.
method: 32 de-identified real patient cases from active clinical practice
Each case paired imaging with a short vignette and a known failure feature
Seven frontier systems were tested and scored by expert review against documented clinical course
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports 224 expert-graded evaluations across 32 cases, with a two-stage review process and preserved replayable conversations.
infographic.watch_item: Because the benchmark is small and intentionally edge-case focused, results may not generalize to routine clinical settings or broader patient populations.
infographic.paper_title: ClinEdge: An Expert-Graded Benchmark of Real Patient Edge Cases Where Frontier Multimodal Models Fail

title: UMCR: Universal Medical Concept Recognition through Guideline Integration and Agentic Linking
authors: Fabrice Lamarche, Amal Zouaq
abstract: Medical Concept Recognition is the task of extracting and grounding spans in medical text to entries in a standard ontology. Current methods are generally developed towards a single ontology and source text type (clinical notes, drug labels, etc.) The central challenge is therefore to build methods that adapt to any target ontology without requiring ontology-specific retraining. More recent approaches like REAL and AutoPCR make direct use of Large Language Models and can theoretically adapt to any ontology choice but suffer from a lack of generalization. We propose UMCR, a pipeline that allows extraction and linking to any target ontology using any source text variety, utilizing direct guideline integration and an agentic linking module. We evaluate our method on the recent MedPath benchmark, covering a wide variety of medical text types and vocabularies, and show that our method achieves strong performance across these tasks. This ability unlocks interoperability in the healthcare domain, allowing for extraction and alignment between different medical standards. Our method also reduces dependence on parametric LLM memory, thanks to improved interaction with the target ontology compared to other proposed approaches.

infographic.key_insight: UMCR is a universal medical concept recognition pipeline that combines guideline integration with agentic linking to map text spans to any target medical ontology.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It could improve interoperability by making it easier to extract and align medical concepts across different document types and standards without ontology-specific retraining.
method: Uses direct guideline integration to guide concept extraction across varied medical text.
Applies an agentic linking module to connect extracted spans to the chosen ontology.
Designed to work across multiple source text varieties and vocabularies.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluated UMCR on the MedPath benchmark spanning diverse medical text types and vocabularies, and report strong performance across these tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may still depend on the quality of ontology interaction and benchmark coverage, so real-world robustness across unseen ontologies or text styles remains a practical concern.
infographic.paper_title: UMCR: Universal Medical Concept Recognition through Guideline Integration and Agentic Linking

title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in Large Language Models
authors: Ziyang Ling
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often diagnose full sight, static clinical cases well yet struggle in foresight, dynamic diagnosis. Prior work has improved this limitation by quantifying the information models acquire and by developing stronger follow-up strategies to improve diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, we introduce a distinctive hindsight to systematically dissect why LLMs fail to acquire diagnostically critical evidence, tracing the failure from evidence identification, utilization and downstream diagnostic updating through not only diagnostic accuracy, but also evidence coverage, trajectory dynamics, and elicited probability and information entropy. Starting experiments from the breakdown at the level of capabilities, to the diagnosis of the pre-event state before the evidence arrives, and to the post-event state transition after the evidence arrives, our research has revealed the profound limitations and internal causes existing in the dynamic diagnostic process. At the same time, we have also conducted sufficient verification and generalization experiments to prove that these limitations are widespread. Together, these findings shift the central challenge from whether LLMs possess relevant clinical knowledge to whether they can identify, acquire, and effectively use the right evidence under clinical diagnosis and conduct a more detailed mechanism analysis to identify the exact location of the capability gap.

infographic.key_insight: This paper shows that large language models can look competent on static clinical cases but fail to identify, use, and update with the right evidence during dynamic diagnosis.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The work helps explain why LLMs may miss important follow-up information in real clinical workflows, highlighting limits in evidence tracking and diagnostic updating.
method: Dissects failure across evidence identification, evidence use, and diagnostic updating.
Evaluates not just accuracy, but also evidence coverage, trajectory dynamics, probability, and information entropy.
Includes breakdown, pre-event, and post-event analyses plus verification and generalization tests.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experiments spanning capability breakdown, pre-event state before evidence arrives, post-event state transition after evidence arrives, and broader verification/generalization analyses.
infographic.watch_item: These findings are diagnostic-system focused and do not imply safe clinical deployment without further validation in real-world settings.
infographic.paper_title: From Hindsight to Foresight: Dissecting Clinical Evidence Acquisition in Large Language Models

title: BrainAid: Efficient Brain Tumor Detection Using Lightweight CNNs and Explainable AI for Resource-Constrained Environments
authors: Sai Sriram Gonthina, Ross Gore, Bikash Chandra Singh, Pronaya Bhattacharya, Sachin Shetty, Abhishek Phadke
abstract: A brain tumor is an unusual growth of cells in the brain that can be cancerous or not, affecting normal brain function and causing serious risk to health. Existing solutions for brain tumor classification, such as expert manual evaluations of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, are generally inconsistent as different professionals have different criteria and can be resource-intensive, leading to delayed diagnoses. Additionally, while deep learning models have demonstrated potential, they typically require significant computational resources, motivating the need for more efficient and accessible diagnostic tools that can be deployed in real-time healthcare settings. To address these limitations, this study presents BrainAid, which makes efficient use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) for effective classification of four-class classification of glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor MRI scans, outperforming all the standard models such as VGG16, Inception-V3, ResNet-50 and so, while integrating Explainable AI (XAI) to improve interpretability. The BrainAid is trained to classify tumors with a high precision of 98%, achieving an F1 score of 98% and an accuracy of 98% using publicly available dataset. The model is deployed on a Raspberry Pi, demonstrating efficiency in low-resource environments. This system shows the feasibility of real-time, edge-based tumor classification, providing quick diagnostic support for medical professionals and enhancing patient care in resource-limited healthcare facilities and underserved areas.

infographic.key_insight: BrainAid uses lightweight CNNs and explainable AI to classify four brain MRI categories accurately while staying suitable for low-resource deployment.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It could support faster, more accessible tumor screening in settings where specialist review or high-end computing is limited.
method: Trains efficient CNN/ViT-based models on public brain MRI scans
Classifies glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no-tumor cases
Adds XAI to make predictions more interpretable and deploys the system on a Raspberry Pi
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 98% precision, 98% F1 score, and 98% accuracy on a publicly available dataset, with performance described as better than standard baseline models.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from a public dataset, so real-world performance, generalizability, and clinical validation in diverse hospital workflows still need confirmation.
infographic.paper_title: BrainAid: Efficient Brain Tumor Detection Using Lightweight CNNs and Explainable AI for Resource-Constrained Environments

title: Robust Detection of Directional Adversarial Attacks in Deep Neural Networks for Radiological Imaging
authors: Tristan Malatyński, Joanna Jaworek-Korjakowska
abstract: Deep learning is now central to radiology, helping detect changes on X-rays, CTs, and MRIs. However, these systems are highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks - small, crafted perturbations that mislead models while appearing unchanged to humans. Such errors risk missed cancers or false positives. Studies show over 90% attack success on medical scans. Almost 30% of US hospitals use AI in imaging in 2023. Thus, an effective method of detecting such attacks and their directionality is crucial to ensure the credibility and reliability of medical systems based on DNNs. We propose a novel detection framework that leverages subsequent attacks using random noise to identify adversarial perturbations. Our approach uses the analysis of variations in the Sigmoid function to distinguish genuine medical images from adversarially manipulated ones. Specifically, we compare prediction differences between clean and attacked images, as well as between different adversarially altered versions, to improve detection accuracy. We evaluated our method on three popular medical datasets including 'Chest X-Ray Images for Classification', 'Retinal Fundus Multi-disease Image Dataset' and 'Brain Tumor Dataset' under various attack scenarios, including random noise. Our framework achieved up to 99.8% ACC in identifying adversarial directional attacks, significantly outperforming existing defense mechanisms. It consistently identified adversarial samples across varying attack strengths while keeping false positives low, showing strong reliability and potential for clinical use. Furthermore, our proposal highlights its potential for real-world deployment.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a way to detect adversarially altered medical images by comparing model responses to clean, attacked, and noise-perturbed inputs, including the attack direction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If reliable, this could help protect radiology AI from hidden manipulations that might cause missed findings or false alarms.
method: Uses subsequent random-noise attacks to probe whether an image is adversarial
Compares prediction changes with a Sigmoid-based variation analysis
Checks differences across clean vs. adversarial versions to flag directional attacks
infographic.evidence_signal: The approach was tested on three medical imaging datasets and reported up to 99.8% accuracy in identifying adversarial directional attacks across multiple attack scenarios.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is reported from abstracted benchmark testing, so real-world robustness and workflow integration still need validation.
infographic.paper_title: Robust Detection of Directional Adversarial Attacks in Deep Neural Networks for Radiological Imaging

title: Chain of Thought Monitoring Can Fail Even When CoT Is Necessary
authors: Lennart Bürger, Piotr Komorowski, Moritz Weckbecker, Evgenii Kortukov, Aakriti Jain, Sebastian Lapuschkin
abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) monitoring is used by frontier labs to detect misbehaviour of AI systems. Yet, its reliability remains poorly understood. We attribute this to the lack of a successful organizing principle that leads to generalizable conclusions about monitoring reliability in different regimes. Recent work attributes monitoring failures to the CoT not being necessary for the answer, and argues that CoT becomes monitorable when it is necessary. We show that this binary necessary/not-necessary organizing principle is too coarse by demonstrating that monitoring failures persist even if the CoT is necessary for the answer. In response, we introduce a more fine-grained organizing principle based on a hierarchy of four CoT necessity levels. Building on this hierarchy, we develop a framework for measuring CoT monitorability at the three lowest levels via intervention experiments. We demonstrate monitoring failures at all three of these levels on realistic, hard prediction tasks. On a difficult medical-diagnosis task, patient sex and a clinical attribute influence the answer in at least 19% and 24% of correct responses with a necessary CoT, respectively, yet their influence is almost never articulated. These results show that even when CoT is necessary, it is not guaranteed to be monitorable.

infographic.key_insight: Even when a chain-of-thought is necessary for the answer, it can still hide the true reasoning and fail to be reliably monitorable.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For AI-assisted medical decision support, this means an apparently explainable model may still conceal important patient factors, creating safety and oversight risks.
method: Introduced a 4-level hierarchy of chain-of-thought necessity.
Defined monitorability measures for the three lowest necessity levels using intervention experiments.
Tested the framework on realistic, hard prediction tasks including a medical-diagnosis task.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the medical task, patient sex and a clinical attribute affected at least 19% and 24% of correct answers, yet these influences were almost never stated in the CoT.
infographic.watch_item: The findings caution that visible reasoning traces should not be treated as sufficient evidence of faithful or complete explanations in deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Chain of Thought Monitoring Can Fail Even When CoT Is Necessary

title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models
authors: S. M. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed
abstract: Automated disease classification from patient-reported symptoms requires balancing the speed of lightweight discriminative models against the contextual understanding and latency costs of autoregressive large language models (LLMs). Decision foundation models offer an alternative by mapping representations directly to candidate classes without free-form text generation. We adapt Clef-Flash, a 9-billion-parameter decision model built on a Qwen3.5 backbone, for 24-class disease classification on the Symptom2Disease benchmark. Using 4-bit quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) with differential learning rates and a stratified split of 960 training and 240 test cases, the model achieves 95.42% diagnostic accuracy and a macro F1 score of 0.9551. This improves upon the reported zero-shot baselines of 61.67% for a remote API and 65.00% for a local unadapted initialization, and outperforms the ClinicalBERT baseline (90.90%). By evaluating candidate logits in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding, inference takes under 80 milliseconds per record on a single GPU, yielding a reported 31-fold speedup over generative LLM baselines. To examine symptom-level evidence, we introduce a Leave-One-Symptom-Out (LOSO) counterfactual perturbation framework. Removing disease-defining symptom clauses in a psoriasis example reduces predicted-class confidence from 100.00% to 0.12% and shifts the prediction to impetigo with 99.59% confidence, while removing secondary systemic symptoms produces less than 0.01% change in confidence. These findings suggest that decision-based architectures can combine the linguistic capabilities of large foundation models with low-latency inference and symptom-level interpretability for clinical triage.

infographic.key_insight: A 9B decision foundation model fine-tuned with QLoRA can classify 24 diseases from symptoms with high accuracy while avoiding autoregressive text generation.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may support faster symptom-based triage with interpretable, symptom-level evidence, but it is a research model rather than a clinical decision tool.
method: Adapted Clef-Flash (Qwen3.5 backbone) using 4-bit QLoRA with differential learning rates
Trained on a stratified 960-case training split and evaluated on 240 test cases
Used leave-one-symptom-out counterfactuals to test which symptom phrases most influenced predictions
infographic.evidence_signal: On Symptom2Disease, the model reached 95.42% accuracy and 0.9551 macro F1, outperforming ClinicalBERT and zero-shot baselines while running in under 80 ms per record.
infographic.watch_item: Performance and explanation quality were shown on a benchmark dataset, so real-world clinical use would need external validation, safety review, and robustness testing.
infographic.paper_title: Toward System One Clinical Intelligence: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Counterfactual Explainability of Decision Foundation Models

title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
authors: Ivana Janíčková, Yen Y. Tan, Thomas H. Helbich, Philipp Seeböck, Julieta Di Marco, Zsuzsanna Bago-Horvath
abstract: Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease. It provides a comprehensive basis for diagnosis and the identification of biological associations linked to progression or treatment response. Established contrastive learning approaches exploit shared information across modalities, but fall short in exploiting complementary, modality-specific signals relevant for a task. Here, we propose a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from instance-specific variation task-irrelevant, allowing complementary signals across modalities to be leveraged for prediction. The method yields benefits even if modalities are missing at test time. We evaluate the method on a treatment response prediction task using medical imaging and RNA data. Empirical comparison with alignment-based and multimodal VAE state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates improved multimodal prediction performance, and consistent benefits for prediction from a single modality after multimodal training. The full code can be found here: https://github.com/cirmuw/SYNPRED.

infographic.key_insight: SYNPRED introduces a synergistic multimodal VAE that separates shared, modality-specific, and task-irrelevant signals so complementary information from different data types can improve prediction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For treatment response prediction, the approach may perform better than alignment-based methods and still help when only one modality is available at test time.
method: Uses a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE)
Disentangles unimodal, multimodal, and instance-specific task-irrelevant variation
Designed to leverage complementary signals from imaging and RNA data for prediction
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports evaluation on a treatment response prediction task with medical imaging and RNA data, showing improved multimodal prediction and consistent gains for single-modality prediction after multimodal training.
infographic.watch_item: Results are promising but come from the abstract’s described evaluation; broader validation across more cohorts, tasks, and missing-data patterns would be needed before general use.
infographic.paper_title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction

title: FOCUS: A Subspecialty Foundation Model for Intraoperative Central Nervous System Pathology
authors: Xing Liu, Yifan Guo, Hongtai Lv, Lei Lou, Yuyi Tan, Jiang Du
abstract: Intraoperative frozen-section diagnosis of central nervous system (CNS) lesions guides surgical decisions but is challenged by artefacts, diagnostic complexity and time constraints. Most pathology foundation models have limited exposure to CNS frozen tissue. Here we present FOCUS, a subspecialty foundation model pretrained on 27,930 frozen-sections enriched for CNS tissue. FOCUS led 11 internal diagnostic and 12 biomarker-prediction tasks, with mean AUCs of 0.969 and 0.877, respectively, retaining leading performance in temporal and external cohorts. To provide more comprehensive diagnostic information, we further organized ten diagnostic tasks into a WHO-aligned diagnostic hierarchy and separately evaluated FOCUS for lymphoma detection, a critical task for intraoperative surgical decision-making. In reader assessments by six neuropathologists, FOCUS assistance enabled junior readers to approach or exceed unassisted senior readers in hierarchical diagnosis and raised junior readers' lymphoma sensitivity from 81.6% to 94.7%. FOCUS could improve diagnostic accuracy and granularity, inform lymphoma-related resection decisions and provide provisional molecular information. Such capabilities highlight the potential of FOCUS to provide robust, clinically actionable support for intraoperative CNS pathology.

infographic.key_insight: FOCUS is a CNS-focused pathology foundation model pretrained on large frozen-section data that improves intraoperative diagnosis and biomarker prediction for brain and spinal tissue.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It may help neuropathologists make faster, more granular surgical decisions during frozen-section evaluation, including better lymphoma detection and provisional molecular guidance.
method: Pretrained on 27,930 frozen-section pathology images enriched for CNS tissue
Evaluated on 11 internal diagnostic tasks and 12 biomarker-prediction tasks
Assessed in WHO-aligned hierarchical diagnosis and reader studies with six neuropathologists
infographic.evidence_signal: Across internal, temporal, and external cohorts, FOCUS achieved mean AUCs of 0.969 for diagnosis and 0.877 for biomarker prediction, and improved junior readers’ lymphoma sensitivity from 81.6% to 94.7%.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is promising, but real-world adoption will depend on prospective validation across diverse institutions, staining quality, and frozen-section artefacts.
infographic.paper_title: FOCUS: A Subspecialty Foundation Model for Intraoperative Central Nervous System Pathology

title: Identifying Family Relationships from Electronic Health Records: A Machine Learning Approach
authors: Pundir, A.; Hill, A.; Kahn, M. G.; Kwan, B. M.; Lindberg, D. M.; Grannis, S. J.; Schleyer, T. K.; Schilling, L. M.; Kautz, S. V.; Ong, T. C.
abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate machine learning methods for automated identification of family relationships from electronic health records (EHRs). We employed Random Forest classifiers to identify five relationship types: Mother-Child, Father-Child, Sibling-Sibling, Twin-Twin, and Partner-Partner, using a four-stage iterative refinement process to improve precision for patient-centered outcomes research (PCOR) and healthcare applications. Materials and MethodsWe used two large-scale Indiana datasets: the Indiana Network for Patient Care (INPC), comprising approximately 15 million unique individuals across approximately 45 million medical records, and the Indiana Natality dataset (birth certificates, 1970-2024), which served as the gold standard. Positive cases were derived by linking verified relationships from Natality records to INPC using a shared Global Identifier. Negative cases were drawn from a three-tier blocking strategy combined with sliding window restriction and similarity scoring, which together reduced the comparison space from over 10{superscript 1} potential pairs to approximately 121 million candidates. Five Random Forest classifiers underwent four-stage iterative refinement: initial training, feature removal for multicollinearity, feature engineering to address systematic errors, and training-data refinement restricted to relationship pairs with at least one shared contact feature. ResultsThe models achieved precision of 0.92 to 1.00, recall of 0.97 to 1.00, and F1 scores of 0.94 to 1.00 across all relationship types (Mother-Child 0.97, Father-Child 0.98, Sibling-Sibling 0.98, Twin-Twin 1.00, Partner-Partner 0.94). Between 15% and 78% of Natality-verified relationships lacked any shared contact information in INPC and were structurally undetectable by record linkage; restricting training and evaluation to linkable pairs improved precision for four of the five models, and training-data refinement improved F1-scores by a further 0.02-0.04 for the Mother-Child, Father-Child, and Sibling models. High-confidence predictions (probability [≥] 0.9) captured 77-99% of true positives. Age difference was the primary predictor for parent-child and twin relationships, while phone number similarity was most important for siblings. DiscussionThe framework identifies family relationships from standard demographic fields available in most EHR systems. The iterative refinement approach shows how systematic error analysis can guide methodological improvements. Training-data refinement addresses a constraint in EHR-based family linkage: not all verified biological relationships have overlapping demographic footprints in healthcare data. Unlike rule-based approaches, the framework provides probability scores that enable configurable deployment thresholds. ConclusionThe Random Forest models demonstrate high performance suitable for large-scale research deployment and are ready for testing in clinical applications rather than immediate widespread clinical use. The methodology can be adapted to other EHR systems, supporting family-centered study design in patient-centered outcomes research.

infographic.key_insight: A machine-learning approach can accurately infer common family relationships from EHR data, enabling automated family linkage for research and health-system use.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Better family relationship identification could strengthen patient-centered outcomes research, pedigree-aware analyses, and downstream care coordination workflows.
method: Trained Random Forest classifiers for five relationship types: mother-child, father-child, sibling-sibling, twin-twin, and partner-partner.
Used Indiana EHR and natality data, with verified natality links as the gold standard and a multi-stage negative-sampling strategy to narrow candidate pairs.
Refined models through iterative feature removal, feature engineering, and training-data restriction to linkable pairs with shared contact features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five relationship models, performance was strong with precision 0.92-1.00, recall 0.97-1.00, and F1 0.94-1.00; high-confidence predictions captured 77-99% of true positives.
infographic.watch_item: A substantial share of true relationships had no shared contact information in the EHR and were structurally undetectable, so real-world performance depends on data completeness and local record structure.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying Family Relationships from Electronic Health Records: A Machine Learning Approach

title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation
authors: Jiaqi Tang, Yu Wang, Yang Liu, Jing Tao, Fandong Zhang, Zhou Zhen
abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires fine-tuning candidates on labelled target data, at substantial computational cost. We benchmark 23 candidates across the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks spanning multiple anatomies and modalities. No candidate ranked among the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder could outperform a transformer trained with the same objective on one task but underperform it on another. We benchmark transferability estimators against the fine-tuned rankings and find that their agreement varies across dense segmentation, classification and regression. InsightRank uses task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank candidates before fine-tuning. Across the 23-model pool, mean Kendall tau-b was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification and regression. The segmentation Top 3 contained a task winner on four of nine tasks; the image-level Top 3 contained none on the five tasks, despite better full-ranking agreement than the matched conventional estimators. A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks. Together, the benchmark provides a common reference for model selection and InsightRank offers a lower-cost way to prioritize fine-tuning, with shortlist performance that differs by target type.

infographic.key_insight: A 23-model benchmark showed that no single self-supervised 3D medical foundation model consistently transfers best across segmentation, classification, and regression tasks, so model choice should be task-specific.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For medical AI deployment, this work helps teams shortlist foundation models more efficiently before fine-tuning, potentially reducing compute while improving selection for the target task.
method: Benchmarked 23 self-supervised 3D foundation models on 14 labeled downstream tasks.
Compared fine-tuned performance across segmentation, classification, and regression, then tested transferability estimators.
Introduced InsightRank, which uses frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank models pre-fine-tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Mean Kendall tau-b agreement with fine-tuned rankings was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification/regression, and a three-model shortlist cut extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability estimates were less reliable for image-level classification/regression than for segmentation, so shortlist rankings still need validation on the intended task and modality.
infographic.paper_title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation

title: Learning to Detect Shifts in Unstructured Data Streams via Monitoring-by-Betting
authors: Siyu Zhou, Jialin Ouyang, Fan Xia, Adarsh Subbaswamy, Drew Prinster, Suchi Saria
abstract: Continuous monitoring of generative AI systems requires detecting distribution shifts in the unstructured data they ingest and generate. Existing monitoring methods typically control false alarms by requiring the discrepancy measure used to detect shifts to be *pre-specified*. However, for unstructured data, pre-specification creates a sensitivity--breadth trade-off: a narrowly defined measure is sensitive to the anticipated shift but may miss unexpected changes, whereas a broadly defined measure may detect a wider range of shifts but with reduced sensitivity. Although adaptively hypothesizing the shift direction can overcome this limitation, such data-dependent adaptation generally invalidates conventional false-alarm guarantees. We reconcile adaptivity with statistical validity through testing-by-betting, reframing sequential changepoint detection as a betting game in which the bettor continually updates its hypothesized shift direction, or witness function, as new observations arrive. We introduce *asymptotic e-detectors*, which approximate the pre-change distribution using a calibration set of size $m$, and prove that they asymptotically control the average run length to a false alarm as $m$ increases. Empirically, calibration sets as small as $m=30$ provide effective control. We then develop adaptive monitoring strategies ranging from black-box bettors that learn from embeddings to interpretable bettors based on LLM-proposed concepts. Across three real-world datasets, including data from a clinical AI scribe deployment, adaptive monitors detect shifts faster than fixed monitors at the same false-alarm level. Further, when the true shifts are sparse and interpretable, LLM-concept monitors provide the fastest and most interpretable detection, while also guiding root-cause diagnosis for complex shifts.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that sequential shift detection in unstructured AI data can stay statistically valid even when the detector adaptively learns what kind of shift to look for.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For clinical AI systems such as AI scribes, this could enable faster and more reliable detection of distribution shifts that may affect system behavior, safety, or downstream workflow quality.
method: Reframes changepoint detection as a testing-by-betting game with an adaptive witness function.
Introduces asymptotic e-detectors that use a calibration set to approximate the pre-change distribution and control false alarms as calibration size grows.
Builds both black-box embedding-based bettors and interpretable LLM-concept bettors for monitoring unstructured data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three real-world datasets, including a clinical AI scribe deployment, the adaptive monitors detected shifts faster than fixed monitors at the same false-alarm level, and calibration sets as small as 30 were effective.
infographic.watch_item: The strongest formal false-alarm guarantees are asymptotic and depend on calibration data quality and whether the observed shift is well captured by the learned witness function.
infographic.paper_title: Learning to Detect Shifts in Unstructured Data Streams via Monitoring-by-Betting

title: More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules
authors: Xiaoqian Lu, Guangfu Guo, Long Cheng, Kunpeng Liu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in clinical decision support. However, existing approaches often rely on multi-step reasoning or multi-agent collaboration to execute clinical guidelines, introducing substantial computational overhead without reliably preventing decision errors. To address these limitations, we propose a framework for Medical Decision Execution (MedDEx) that integrates structured patient states with deterministic rule execution to support guideline-based treatment planning. MedDEx separates clinical record interpretation from guideline execution, leveraging LLMs to extract patient information and generate treatment plans while assigning guideline-defined decision logic to a rule executor. Experiments across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks demonstrate that MedDEx improves decision accuracy while reducing inference costs. Further analyses highlight the critical roles of structured patient representations and deterministic rule execution, suggesting that additional LLM reasoning does not necessarily translate into better guideline adherence.

infographic.key_insight: MedDEx shows that for guideline-based clinical decisions, combining LLM-based patient-state extraction with deterministic rule execution can be more accurate and efficient than adding more LLM reasoning steps.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could improve treatment-planning support by making guideline adherence more reliable while lowering computational cost.
method: LLM extracts structured patient state from clinical records.
A deterministic rule engine executes guideline-defined decision logic.
LLM helps generate plans, but does not replace the rule-based decision step.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework was evaluated across multiple clinical guideline benchmarks and reported higher decision accuracy with lower inference costs.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on accurate patient-state extraction and well-specified rules, so errors in either component could affect real-world deployment.
infographic.paper_title: More Reasoning Is Not Always Better: Executing Clinical Guidelines with LLMs and Rules
